This is a review of Modern Optics from the Spring 2026 semester, taught by Professor Dai Ya'nan, with reference to Hecht's Optics (5th Edition).

This is an exam-focused review: it only covers the key topics mentioned in Professor Dai's review lectures, and many derivations that I find obvious have been omitted. For a systematic study of optics, consulting a textbook is still recommended.

I don't particularly recommend reading Hecht directly — its sign conventions are highly complex, sometimes even self-contradictory, and much of the content is unnecessary. It reads more like a popular science book than a textbook.

Chapters 1 and 2 are too simple and are omitted.

Chapter 3: Electromagnetic Theory, Photons, and Light​

3.1 Basic Definitions​

Irradiance​

Irradiance III is the average energy transported by an electromagnetic wave per unit area per unit time. For a harmonic wave in vacuum, the magnitude of the time-averaged Poynting vector is the irradiance (unit: W/m2\mathrm{W/m^2}W/m2):

I=⟨S⟩T=c2ϵ0 ∣E⃗0×B⃗0∣  ⟨cos⁡2(k⃗⋅r⃗−ωt)⟩=c2ϵ02 ∣E⃗0×B⃗0∣I = \langle S \rangle_{T} = c^{2}\epsilon_{0}\,|\vec{E}_{0}\times \vec{B}_{0}|\;\langle \cos^{2}(\vec{k}\cdot \vec{r} -\omega t)\rangle = \frac{c^{2}\epsilon_{0}}{2}\,|\vec{E}_{0}\times \vec{B}_{0}|I=⟨S⟩T​=c2ϵ0​∣E0​×B0​∣⟨cos2(k⋅r−ωt)⟩=2c2ϵ0​​∣E0​×B0​∣

In vacuum, ∣B⃗0∣=∣E⃗0∣/c|\vec{B}_{0}| = |\vec{E}_{0}|/c∣B0​∣=∣E0​∣/c, so the irradiance is proportional to the square of the electric field amplitude:

I=⟨S⟩T=c ϵ02 E02I = \langle S \rangle_{T} = \frac{c\,\epsilon_{0}}{2}\,E_{0}^{2}I=⟨S⟩T​=2cϵ0​​E02​

The power PPP (in watts) passing through an area AAA is

P=IA[W=J/s]P = IA \qquad [\mathrm{W} = \mathrm{J/s}]P=IA[W=J/s]

Spherical Waves​

A point source in a homogeneous medium radiates spherical waves. From the scalar wave equation:

E(r,t)=(Ar)cos⁡(kr∓ωt)E(r,t) = \left(\frac{\mathcal{A}}{r}\right)\cos(kr \mp \omega t)E(r,t)=(rA​)cos(kr∓ωt)

where A\mathcal{A}A is the source strength. At any distance rrr, rE0(r)=constrE_0(r) = \text{const}rE0​(r)=const. Thus the amplitude decreases inversely with rrr, and the irradiance of a point source follows the inverse-square law:

I∝1r2.I \propto \frac{1}{r^{2}}.I∝r21​.

Note that spherical electromagnetic waves do not actually exist in reality. This is because Gauss's law ∇⋅E⃗=ρϵ\nabla \cdot \vec{E} = \dfrac{\rho}{\epsilon}∇⋅E=ϵρ​ forcibly erases all differences in charge distribution — it is impossible to construct a charge distribution and motion that produces a spherical wave. Of course, it remains an excellent approximation.

Photon Flux​

For a quasi-monochromatic beam of cross-sectional area AAA, the average photon flux (photons per second) is

Φ=AIhν0\Phi = \frac{AI}{h\nu_0}Φ=hν0​AI​

A single photon carries energy E=hνE = h\nuE=hν (hhh is Planck's constant). Numerically, a P=1P = 1P=1 mW He–Ne laser (λ=632.8  nm\lambda = 632.8\;\mathrm{nm}λ=632.8nm) emits approximately Φ≈3.2×1015\Phi \approx 3.2 \times 10^{15}Φ≈3.2×1015 photons per second.

Radiation Pressure​

Maxwell showed that electromagnetic radiation carries momentum. The instantaneous radiation pressure equals the energy density:

Pr=uE+uB=S(t)cP_r = u_E + u_B = \frac{S(t)}{c}Pr​=uE​+uB​=cS(t)​

The average radiation pressure on a perfectly absorbing surface is

⟨Pr⟩=⟨S(t)⟩c=Ic\langle P_r \rangle = \frac{\langle S(t) \rangle}{c} = \frac{I}{c}⟨Pr​⟩=c⟨S(t)⟩​=cI​

Unit: [Pr]=W m−2/m s−1=N m−2 (pascals)[P_r] = \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}} / \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} = \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}} \,(\text{pascals})[Pr​]=Wm−2/ms−1=Nm−2(pascals).

The force on an absorbing area AAA is F=APrF = AP_rF=APr​. Assuming the volume density of electromagnetic momentum is pvp_vpv​, we have:

F=pv⋅cΔtAΔt,F = \frac{p_v \cdot c\Delta t A}{\Delta t},F=Δtpv​⋅cΔtA​,

Solving simultaneously yields:

pv=Sc2p_v = \frac{S}{c^2}pv​=c2S​

In the photon picture, each quantum carries momentum

p=Ec=hλ=ℏkp = \frac{E}{c} = \frac{h}{\lambda} = \hbar kp=cE​=λh​=ℏk

3.2 Light in Matter​

In a medium with no free charges or currents, that is homogeneous, isotropic, and has linear constitutive relations, Maxwell's equations reduce to:

∇2E⃗=μϵ∂E⃗∂t,∇2B⃗=μϵ∂B⃗∂t,\nabla^2 \vec{E} = \mu \epsilon \frac{\partial{\vec{E}}}{\partial t}, \qquad \nabla^2 \vec{B} = \mu \epsilon \frac{\partial{\vec{B}}}{\partial t},∇2E=μϵ∂t∂E​,∇2B=μϵ∂t∂B​,

These are classical wave equations, with traveling wave solutions:

E⃗(r⃗,t)=E⃗0ei(k⃗⋅r⃗−ωt),B⃗(r⃗,t)=1v(k^×E⃗),\vec{E}(\vec{r}, t) = \vec{E}_0 e^{i\left(\vec{k}\cdot \vec{r} - \omega t\right)}, \qquad \vec{B}(\vec{r}, t) = \frac{1}{v}\left(\hat{k} \times \vec{E}\right),E(r,t)=E0​ei(k⋅r−ωt),B(r,t)=v1​(k^×E),

Here we used the other two Maxwell equations to simplify. This requires electromagnetic waves to be transverse.

Define the phase velocity as the speed at which a surface of constant phase kx−ωt=constkx-\omega t=\text{const}kx−ωt=const moves:

vp=dxdt=ωk,v_p = \frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{\omega}{k},vp​=dtdx​=kω​,

Substituting the solution into Maxwell's equations proves that vp=1μϵv_p = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu\epsilon}}vp​=μϵ​1​. In particular, the speed of light in vacuum is c=1μ0ϵ0c = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\epsilon_0}}c=μ0​ϵ0​​1​.

The (absolute) refractive index is defined as

n≡cvp=cωk=ϵμϵ0μ0n \equiv \frac{c}{v_p} = \frac{c}{\omega}k = \sqrt{\frac{\epsilon\mu}{\epsilon_0\mu_0}}n≡vp​c​=ωc​k=ϵ0​μ0​ϵμ​​

For non-magnetic materials (μ≈μ0\mu \approx \mu_0μ≈μ0​), this simplifies to

n=ϵϵ0=KE\boxed{n = \sqrt{\frac{\epsilon}{\epsilon_0}} = \sqrt{K_E}}n=ϵ0​ϵ​​=KE​​​

where KEK_EKE​ is the dielectric constant: ϵ=KEϵ0\epsilon = K_E \epsilon_0ϵ=KE​ϵ0​.

The dielectric constant depends on the frequency of light: KE=KE(ω)K_E=K_E(\omega)KE​=KE​(ω), so the phase velocity and refractive index are also frequency-dependent — this is called dispersion.

Origin of the Term "Dispersion"

Why is it called "dispersion" (chromatic dispersion)? Imagine: for the same wave vector kkk, light of different frequencies has different phase velocities vp(ω)v_p(\omega)vp​(ω), and the dependence is positively correlated — lower-frequency light is slower, higher-frequency light is faster. And frequency corresponds to the color of light: low-frequency light is red, high-frequency light is violet. Thus, in a medium, different colors gradually separate over time. This is chromatic "dispersion." The concept has been generalized to many other fields, even though those fields involve no colors at all.

Terminology Convention

Hecht's book calls ϵ\epsilonϵ the "capacitivity" and KEK_EKE​ the "dielectric constant" — a convention that differs from standard practice and is rather uninteresting.

Group Velocity​

Given the dispersion relation for electromagnetic waves in a medium:

ω=vpk=cn(ω)k,\omega = v_p k = \frac{c}{n(\omega)}k,ω=vp​k=n(ω)c​k,

Differentiating with respect to kkk yields:

dωdk=cn(ω)−ckn2(ω)dndk=1n(ω)(c−ωdndωdωdk)\frac{\mathrm{d}\omega}{\mathrm{d}k} = \frac{c}{n(\omega)} - \frac{ck}{n^2(\omega)}\frac{\mathrm{d}n}{\mathrm{d}k} = \frac{1}{n(\omega)}\left(c - \omega\frac{\mathrm{d}n}{\mathrm{d}\omega}\frac{\mathrm{d}\omega}{\mathrm{d}k}\right)dkdω​=n(ω)c​−n2(ω)ck​dkdn​=n(ω)1​(c−ωdωdn​dkdω​)

Defining the group velocity vg=dωdkv_g = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}\omega}{\mathrm{d} k}vg​=dkdω​, we solve to obtain:

vg=cn(ω)+ωdndω.v_g = \cfrac{c}{n(\omega) + \omega\cfrac{\mathrm{d}n}{\mathrm{d}\omega}}.vg​=n(ω)+ωdωdn​c​.

This describes the propagation speed of a wave packet (its center), which can, under certain exotic dispersion relations, exceed the speed of light.

Lorentz Oscillator Model​

In the classical picture, bound electrons respond to the driving electric field as damped harmonic oscillators. Let there be NNN molecules per unit volume, each with ZZZ electrons, and each transition jjj has a natural frequency ω0j\omega_{0j}ω0j​ and oscillator strength fjf_jfj​:

n2(ω)=1+Nqe2ϵ0me∑jfjω0j2−ω2,∑jfj=Z.n^{2}(\omega) = 1 + \frac{N q_e^{2}}{\epsilon_0 m_e} \sum_{j} \frac{f_j}{\omega_{0j}^{2} - \omega^{2}}, \qquad \sum_j f_j = Z.n2(ω)=1+ϵ0​me​Nqe2​​j∑​ω0j2​−ω2fj​​,j∑​fj​=Z.
  • Normal dispersion: far from resonance, nnn increases with ω\omegaω.
  • Anomalous dispersion: near the resonance frequency, nnn decreases with increasing ω\omegaω, and strong absorption occurs here. The simple undamped model diverges at ω=ω0j\omega = \omega_{0j}ω=ω0j​; actual treatment requires adding a damping term ∝γ dr/dt\propto \gamma\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}/\mathrm{d}t∝γdr/dt to keep nnn finite.

Slightly above the resonance frequency, the dielectric function can become negative (e.g., in metals below the plasma frequency, or in certain metamaterials). This leads to phenomena such as total external reflection and the possibility of negative refraction.

Chapter 4: Propagation of Light​

4.1 Reflection and Refraction​

Huygens' Principle​

Huygens' Principle states that every point on a wavefront can be regarded as a source of secondary spherical wavelets, and the new wavefront at any later time is the envelope of these wavelets.

Huygens' Principle can be used to prove the law of reflection and Snell's law.

Fermat's Principle​

Let light propagate along a path CCC in a (inhomogeneous) medium with refractive index n(r⃗)n(\vec{r})n(r). The optical path length is defined as the integral of the refractive index along the path:

OPL=∫Cn(r⃗) ds\text{OPL} = \int_C n(\vec{r}) \, \mathrm{d}sOPL=∫C​n(r)ds

where dsdsds is the arc-length element of the path. Its physical meaning:

n(r⃗) ds=cvp(r⃗) ds=c dtvp(r⃗)dsdt=c dt,n(\vec{r})\,\mathrm{d}s = \frac{c}{v_p(\vec{r})}\,\mathrm{d}s = \frac{c\,\mathrm{d}t}{v_p(\vec{r})}\frac{\mathrm{d}s}{\mathrm{d}t} = c\,\mathrm{d}t,n(r)ds=vp​(r)c​ds=vp​(r)cdt​dtds​=cdt,

That is, the optical path length is the distance light would travel in vacuum in the same amount of time.

Fermat's Principle: the actual path taken by light between two points AAA and BBB makes the optical path length stationary, i.e., the first-order variation of the optical path length is zero:

δ∫ABn ds=0\delta\int_A^B n\,\mathrm{d}s = 0δ∫AB​nds=0

Usually it is a minimum, but in some cases it can be a maximum or a saddle point. For example, light reflecting off a concave mirror may correspond to a maximum optical path; straight-line propagation in a homogeneous medium corresponds to a minimum optical path.

From Fermat's Principle one can derive the law of reflection, Snell's law, and the curved trajectories of light in inhomogeneous media.

Law of Reflection​

Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection: θi=θr\theta_i = \theta_rθi​=θr​.

Snell's Law and Total Internal Reflection​

At the interface between two media with refractive indices nin_ini​ and ntn_tnt​:

nisin⁡θi=ntsin⁡θtn_i \sin\theta_i = n_t \sin\theta_tni​sinθi​=nt​sinθt​

Equivalently,

sin⁡θisin⁡θt=ntni≡nti\frac{\sin\theta_i}{\sin\theta_t} = \frac{n_t}{n_i} \equiv n_{ti}sinθt​sinθi​​=ni​nt​​≡nti​

where ntin_{ti}nti​ is the relative refractive index of medium ttt with respect to medium iii.

When going from an optically denser to a rarer medium (ni>ntn_i > n_tni​>nt​), Snell's law gives sin⁡θt=(ni/nt)sin⁡θi\sin\theta_t = (n_i/n_t) \sin\theta_isinθt​=(ni​/nt​)sinθi​. If sin⁡θi\sin\theta_isinθi​ exceeds nt/nin_t/n_int​/ni​, no real θt\theta_tθt​ exists, hence no refracted wave — the wave is totally internally reflected back into the denser medium.

The critical angle is defined as

sin⁡θc=ntni=nti\sin\theta_c = \frac{n_t}{n_i} = n_{ti}sinθc​=ni​nt​​=nti​

At this angle θt=90∘\theta_t = 90^{\circ}θt​=90∘, and the wave propagates exactly along the interface.

4.2 Fresnel Equations​

Using electrodynamics, we can compute the amplitude of the transmitted and reflected waves, which depends on the polarization state. Let the wave be E⃗a=E⃗0aei(k⃗a⋅r⃗−ωt)\vec{E}_a = \vec{E}_{0a}e^{i\left(\vec{k}_a \cdot \vec{r} - \omega t\right)}Ea​=E0a​ei(ka​⋅r−ωt), where a=ia = ia=i for the incident wave, rrr for the reflected wave, and ttt for the transmitted wave.

Electrodynamics guarantees that the frequency ω\omegaω is the same for all three waves, and that the electric field completely determines the magnetic field: B⃗(r⃗,t)=1v(k⃗×E⃗)\vec{B}(\vec{r}, t) = \dfrac{1}{v}\left(\vec{k} \times \vec{E}\right)B(r,t)=v1​(k×E); choosing the origin at the point of incidence eliminates any extra phase for the reflected and transmitted waves.

Define:

rk=(E0rE0i)k,tk=(E0tE0i)kr_k = \left(\frac{E_{0r}}{E_{0i}}\right)_k, \qquad t_k = \left(\frac{E_{0t}}{E_{0i}}\right)_krk​=(E0i​E0r​​)k​,tk​=(E0i​E0t​​)k​

where kkk can be ⊥\perp⊥, meaning the electric field is perpendicular to the plane of incidence; or ∥\parallel∥, meaning the electric field is parallel to the plane of incidence. See the figures for reference.

  1. TM polarization (EEE parallel to the plane of incidence):
r∥=ntμtcos⁡θi−niμicos⁡θtniμicos⁡θt+ntμtcos⁡θit∥=2niμicos⁡θintμtcos⁡θi+niμicos⁡θtr_{\parallel} = \cfrac{\cfrac{n_t}{\mu_t} \cos\theta_i - \cfrac{n_i}{\mu_i} \cos\theta_t}{\cfrac{n_i}{\mu_i} \cos\theta_t + \cfrac{n_t}{\mu_t} \cos\theta_i} \qquad t_{\parallel} = \cfrac{2\cfrac{n_i}{\mu_i} \cos\theta_i}{\cfrac{n_t}{\mu_t} \cos\theta_i + \cfrac{n_i}{\mu_i} \cos\theta_t}r∥​=μi​ni​​cosθt​+μt​nt​​cosθi​μt​nt​​cosθi​−μi​ni​​cosθt​​t∥​=μt​nt​​cosθi​+μi​ni​​cosθt​2μi​ni​​cosθi​​

Note: the sign of rrr depends on the choice of direction for the reflected EEE field in the derivation. We follow the convention of Hecht's Optics (5th Edition), as shown in the figures.

For non-magnetic media (μi≈μt≈1\mu_i\approx\mu_t\approx 1μi​≈μt​≈1), the Fresnel equations simplify to:

r⊥=nicos⁡θi−ntcos⁡θtnicos⁡θi+ntcos⁡θtt⊥=2nicos⁡θinicos⁡θi+ntcos⁡θtr_{\perp} = \frac{n_i \cos\theta_i - n_t \cos\theta_t}{n_i \cos\theta_i + n_t \cos\theta_t} \qquad t_{\perp} = \frac{2n_i \cos\theta_i}{n_i \cos\theta_i + n_t \cos\theta_t}r⊥​=ni​cosθi​+nt​cosθt​ni​cosθi​−nt​cosθt​​t⊥​=ni​cosθi​+nt​cosθt​2ni​cosθi​​ r∥=ntcos⁡θi−nicos⁡θtnicos⁡θt+ntcos⁡θit∥=2nicos⁡θinicos⁡θt+ntcos⁡θir_{\parallel} = \frac{n_t \cos\theta_i - n_i \cos\theta_t}{n_i \cos\theta_t + n_t \cos\theta_i} \qquad t_{\parallel} = \frac{2n_i \cos\theta_i}{n_i \cos\theta_t + n_t \cos\theta_i}r∥​=ni​cosθt​+nt​cosθi​nt​cosθi​−ni​cosθt​​t∥​=ni​cosθt​+nt​cosθi​2ni​cosθi​​

Using Snell's law, the above can be further simplified to:

r⊥=−sin⁡(θi−θt)sin⁡(θi+θt)t⊥=+2sin⁡θtcos⁡θisin⁡(θi+θt)r_{\perp} = -\frac{\sin(\theta_i-\theta_t)}{\sin(\theta_i+\theta_t)} \qquad t_{\perp} = +\frac{2\sin\theta_t\cos\theta_i}{\sin(\theta_i+\theta_t)}r⊥​=−sin(θi​+θt​)sin(θi​−θt​)​t⊥​=+sin(θi​+θt​)2sinθt​cosθi​​ r∥=+tan⁡(θi−θt)tan⁡(θi+θt)t∥=+2sin⁡θtcos⁡θisin⁡(θi+θt)cos⁡(θi−θt)r_{\parallel} = +\frac{\tan(\theta_i-\theta_t)}{\tan(\theta_i+\theta_t)} \qquad t_{\parallel} = +\frac{2\sin\theta_t\cos\theta_i}{\sin(\theta_i+\theta_t)\cos(\theta_i-\theta_t)}r∥​=+tan(θi​+θt​)tan(θi​−θt​)​t∥​=+sin(θi​+θt​)cos(θi​−θt​)2sinθt​cosθi​​

They represent power (irradiance) ratios. Under lossless conditions, R+T=1R+T=1R+T=1, i.e., energy conservation.

4.3 Evanescent Waves​

Under total internal reflection, a transmitted wave actually still exists:

The wave vector of the transmitted wave: k⃗t=(ktx,kty,0)\vec{k}_t = (k_{tx}, k_{ty}, 0)kt​=(ktx​,kty​,0). From the geometry shown in the figure:

ktx=ktsin⁡θt,kty=ktcos⁡θt,k_{tx} = k_t \sin{\theta_t}, \qquad k_{ty} = k_t \cos{\theta_t},ktx​=kt​sinθt​,kty​=kt​cosθt​,

For total internal reflection, we cannot determine θt\theta_tθt​, so we seek an equivalent formulation of Snell's law to express all quantities involving θt\theta_tθt​ in terms of θi\theta_iθi​:

nisin⁡θi=ntsin⁡θt⟹nicos⁡θi=ntcos⁡θt,n_i \sin\theta_i = n_t \sin\theta_t \Longrightarrow n_i \cos\theta_i = n_t \cos\theta_t,ni​sinθi​=nt​sinθt​⟹ni​cosθi​=nt​cosθt​,

That is:

ntcos⁡θt=ni1−sin⁡2θt=ni1−sin⁡2θinti2n_t\cos\theta_t = n_i\sqrt{1-\sin^2\theta_t} = n_i\sqrt{1-\frac{\sin^2\theta_i}{n_{ti}^2}}nt​cosθt​=ni​1−sin2θt​​=ni​1−nti2​sin2θi​​​

Since n=cvp=cωkn = \dfrac{c}{v_p} = \dfrac{c}{\omega} kn=vp​c​=ωc​k, we have:

ky=ktcos⁡θt=ki1−sin⁡2θinti2,kx=ktsin⁡θintik_y = k_t\cos\theta_t = k_i\sqrt{1-\frac{\sin^2\theta_i}{n_{ti}^2}}, \qquad k_x = k_t \frac{\sin\theta_i}{n_{ti}}ky​=kt​cosθt​=ki​1−nti2​sin2θi​​​,kx​=kt​nti​sinθi​​

The above discussion holds for arbitrary angles of incidence. Now consider the case where the incident angle exceeds the critical angle and total internal reflection occurs:

sin⁡θt=sin⁡θinti≥1,\sin\theta_t = \frac{\sin\theta_i}{n_{ti}} \geq 1,sinθt​=nti​sinθi​​≥1,

yielding:

kty=iktsin⁡2θinti2−1≡iβk_{ty} = ik_t\sqrt{\frac{\sin^2\theta_i}{n_{ti}^2} - 1} \equiv i\betakty​=ikt​nti2​sin2θi​​−1​≡iβ

where the attenuation coefficient is defined as:

β=ktsin⁡2θinti2−1.\beta = k_t \sqrt{\frac{\sin^{2}\theta_i}{n_{ti}^{2}} - 1}.β=kt​nti2​sin2θi​​−1​.

kxk_xkx​ remains unchanged. Thus, the transmitted wave can be written as:

That is, the amplitude decays exponentially with distance yyy from the interface. The penetration depth is defined as δ=1/β\delta = 1/\betaδ=1/β, at which the amplitude has decayed to 1/e1/e1/e of its initial value. The penetration depth is typically on the order of one wavelength.

Frustrated Total Internal Reflection (FTIR)​

If a denser medium is placed very close to the interface — so close that the evanescent wave still retains a significant amplitude — the evanescent field can couple energy across the gap, producing a propagating electromagnetic wave in the new denser medium. This effect is analogous to quantum tunneling, with transmission coefficient T∝e−2βdT \propto e^{-2\beta d}T∝e−2βd.

Chapter 5: Geometrical Optics​

Monochromatic light does not exist in nature. In any case, the light emitted by a source always consists of wave packets of similar frequencies, emitted over a finite duration.

Uniaxial Crystals​

The most important type of birefringent crystal is the uniaxial crystal (e.g., calcite CaCO3_33​), which has a special direction called the optic axis; light propagating along this direction experiences no birefringence. In other words, a uniaxial crystal has rotational symmetry about the optic axis.

When a beam of unpolarized light is incident on a uniaxial crystal, it splits into two beams with mutually orthogonal polarizations:

9.4 Interferometers (Michelson)​

The Michelson interferometer splits a light beam, sends the two parts along different paths, and then recombines them. A compensating plate (identical to the beam splitter) ensures that both beams pass through the same thickness of glass, balancing dispersion so that white-light fringes can be observed. The fringe pattern can reveal optical path differences as small as a fraction of a wavelength, making the Michelson interferometer an extremely sensitive measurement tool.
